food.text: For the Aztecs, maize was the food without which a meal was not a meal, much as wheat was in much of Europe or rice in most of East Asia. It came in varieties that differed in color, texture, size and prestige. People ate it as corn tortillas, tamales or ātōlli, a maize gruel.

Aztec elites took pride in not drinking pulque, the fermented juice of the century plant, or maguey, which was a drink of commoners. They preferred cacao drinks, among the most prestigious luxuries available. Drinking was tolerated, but becoming intoxicated was not, and the penalties were very stiff and stricter for the elite. A commoner's first offense was punished by tearing his house down and sending him off to live in the field like an animal, while a noble generally got no second chance and could be executed for overindulging.

The Aztec diet rested on maize, beans and squash, often with chilis, nopales and tomatoes added. New World grains such as amaranth and chia rounded it out. Combined with maize, these basic foods would have provided the average diet.

Cooking maize grains in alkaline solutions, a process called nixtamalization, significantly raised the nutritional value of the common staple. Aztec cooks relied on this method for their basic foods, including the dough behind tortillas and tamales.

Although the Aztec diet was mostly vegetarian, Aztecs ate insects such as grasshoppers, called chapulines, along with maguey worm, ants and larvae. The article notes that insects have a higher protein content than meat. Even now they are considered a delicacy in some parts of Mexico.

Cacao drinks were made by grinding toasted cacao beans, sometimes with parched corn, and mixing the powder with water. The mixture was beaten with a wooden whisk until foamy, and vanilla orchid pods or honey were added as flavor enhancers.
The Aztecs also harvested acocils, a small and abundant crayfish of Lake Texcoco. They gathered Spirulina algae too, making it into a sort of cake called tecuitlatl that was rich in flavonoids.

The main Aztec cooking method was boiling or steaming in two-handled clay pots called xoctli in Nahuatl. To steam tamales, a cook poured a little water into the pot and set the husk-wrapped tamales on a light structure of twigs in the middle. The pots were also used to prepare nixtamal, beans, stews and hot beverages.
Chocolate was seen as an energy drink and a libido increaser. Moctezuma II was recorded as drinking 50 cups a day from a golden goblet.

Aztec influence may have popularized the tortilla among the Maya, who previously did not have it. As Maya city-states saw Aztec influence, tortillas became as important as tamales. In Yucatán, the Maya ate tortillas with beans and chile sauce for dinner, their only solid meal.

The Mixtec city of Tututepec in Oaxaca had high tortilla production, as shown by the archaeological presence of comals. Its people ate tortillas on their own or used them to pick up beans, vegetables, or, less commonly, meat. The Zapotec of Oaxaca ate theirs with meat or fish.

In the Caribbean, historian James Delbourgo says the Taínos practiced the brewing of cocoa beans as far back as 1494. This practice led to the recipe for chocolate milk and traditional Jamaican chocolate tea.
The Otomi of Central Mexico built rituals around corn. They painted tortillas for ceremonies, at first using imagery from their own religion.

art.text: The Toltec culture ruled a state centered in Tula, Hidalgo, reaching prominence from 950 to 1150 AD. In the Nahuatl language, the word Tōltēkatl came to take on the meaning "artisan", tying the name of this people to skilled craftsmanship.

The buildings of Chichen Itza show many architectural and iconographic elements that some historians have called Mexicanized. Influences from central Mexico mix with the Puuc style of the upper peninsula in its Classic Maya architecture.

Some archaeologists, such as Richard Diehl, argue for a Toltec archaeological horizon, a set of stylistic traits associated with Tula that spread to other Mesoamerican cultures. Its traits include Tohil plumbate ceramic ware and Silho or X-Fine Orange Ware ceramics.

Stylistic traits associated with Tula also appear in Chichén Itzá, and scholars have long argued over why. Some propose a Toltec military conquest of Chichén Itzá, others say Chichén Itzá established Tula as a colony, and others see only loose connections between the two.

The Toltec-like elements at Chichen Itza were recently conjectured to result from a mass migration or conquest by Toltec groups. However, recent studies suggest they may instead express a prestigious and widespread political system during the Early Postclassic in Mesoamerica.

The later Aztec culture considered the Toltec its intellectual and cultural predecessors. The Aztecs described Toltec culture emanating from Tōllān, the Nahuatl name for Tula, as the epitome of civilization.
Traits linked to the Toltec horizon include the Mixtec-Puebla style of iconography. Scholars dispute whether the Mixteca-Puebla art style has any meaning at all.

Researchers have not reached a consensus on why Tula and the Maya site of Chichén Itzá look so alike in architecture and iconography. They also disagree about the degree and direction of influence between the two. Florescano adds that Mayan sources refer to Chichén Itzá when speaking of the mythical place Zuyua, also called Tollan.

war.text: By the time of the Spanish conquest, the macuahuitl was widely distributed across Mesoamerica and served as a standard close-combat weapon. Records show its use by the Aztecs, Mixtecs, Tarascans and Toltecs, among others. In one account, an Indian warrior struck a Spanish rider's horse in the breast so that he opened it to the entrails, and it fell dead on the spot; the Spaniard who recorded it said the stone blades cut like a Toledo blade. Metal swords brought Mesoamerican auxiliaries in Spanish service more prestige than these obsidian weapons.

The Aztec Empire began as a Triple Alliance of three Nahua city-states: Mexico-Tenochtitlan, Tetzcoco and Tlacopan. It ruled the Valley of Mexico from 1428 and waged wars of conquest. Mexica warfare focused on capturing enemies alive, because prisoners supplied the human sacrifices the Mexica believed were needed to sustain divine favor, though battles could still involve significant killing. When Ahuitzotl conquered the border city of Otzoma, its population was either killed or dispersed.

The macuahuitl was a wooden sword with several embedded obsidian blades, and it served as a standard close-combat weapon. Its name comes from Nahuatl and means "hand-wood". Obsidian can produce an edge sharper than high quality steel razor blades, so the weapon could inflict serious lacerations and was sharp enough to decapitate a man.

Historians once presented the Postclassic period as dominated by warlike states, in contrast to pacifist Classic ones. War became economically advantageous, since defeated polities paid tribute of corn, pumpkin, chili and beans. Leaders were often both head priest and military leader.

Maya warfare was not primarily aimed at territorial expansion. Recent scholarship argues it focused on capturing prisoners and imposing tributary relationships, and one of its main goals may have been to acquire victims for sacrifice. Captives of high value were sacrificed, which the article says was the main reason and prospect for war. Competition over water, farmland and obsidian also drove conflict.

The alliance was formed from the victorious factions of a civil war fought between the city of Azcapotzalco and its former tributary provinces. Although it began as three self-governed city-states, Tenochtitlan became dominant militarily.

Much Maya fighting was at close range, with thrusting, stabbing and crushing. Although bows and arrows were used, spears and the macuahuitl remained much more common. One estimate puts about 500 to 1000 men on the battlefield on each side at most, given the logistics of travel.

In 1479 Axayacatl launched a major invasion of the Purépecha Empire with 32,000 Aztec soldiers. The Purépecha met them just across the border with 50,000 soldiers and scored a resounding victory, killing or capturing over 90% of the Aztec army. Axayacatl himself was wounded in the battle, retreated to Tenochtitlan, and never engaged the Purépecha in battle again.

By the time of the Spanish conquest, the macuahuitl was widely used in Mesoamerica, with records of its use by the Aztecs, Mixtecs, Tarascans, Toltecs and others. Bernal Díaz del Castillo described Pedro de Morón charging into the enemy ranks with three other horsemen: the Indians seized his lance, cut him badly with their broadswords, slashed at his mare, and cut his head off at the neck, and he fell dead. Several obsidian mines lay near the Valley of Mexico, including the Sierra de las Navajas, or Razor Mountains.

Scholars believe raiding was a distinct and widespread form of Maya warfare. Small raiding parties aimed to strike fast and hit targeted sites before defenders could mobilize, a pattern consistent with the archaeological record.

literature.text: Mixtec writing began as a logographic system during the Post-Classic period, which dates from 1000 CE. Mixtec codices recorded genealogy, historic events and cultural narratives. After the Spanish arrived in 1520 AD, the Church, knowing of the religious motifs and creation myths recorded in these codices, confiscated and destroyed them, and it is believed many more codices existed before the Colonial period.

The Dresden Codex is a Maya book from the region of Chichén Itza, dating to the 11th or 12th century. It was long believed to be the oldest surviving book written in the Americas. In 2018 the Maya Codex of Mexico, formerly the Grolier Codex, was proven older by about a century.

The epic history of Lord Eight Deer, whose personal name is Jaguar Claw, is told in several Mixtec codices, including the Codex Bodley and Codex Zouche-Nuttall. He was named after the day on which he was born. He successfully conquered and united most of the Mixteca region.

Mixtec codices were written on decorated strips of bark and animal hide. Some were made by folding bark over into an accordion-like book. Others were made by covering strips of bark and leather with plaster to form a smooth writing surface.

The Dresden Codex contains astronomical and astrological tables, religious references, and information on illness and medicine. It also records conjunctions of planets and moons. It is written in Mayan hieroglyphs.

The Codex Zouche-Nuttall was probably made in the 14th century from 47 sections of animal skin. It records the genealogies, alliances and conquests of 11th- and 12th-century rulers of the Tilantongo kingdom, especially the warrior Lord Eight Deer Jaguar Claw.

Codex Vindobonensis Mexicanus I is an accordion-folded Mixtec book from the 14th century, with 52 pages and a length of 13.5 metres. It opens with mythological genealogies of gods. It also contains lists of Mixtec rulers and priests.

The Dresden Codex pages are made of amate, paper from the pounded inner bark of a wild fig, Ficus cotinifolia. The Maya word for it, hu'un, became equivalent to "book". Unfolded, the accordion-style codex is 3.7 metres long.

During the Post-Classic, Mixtec influences permeated neighboring cultures, reversing earlier periods when others influenced the Mixtec. This sharing of culture also appears in writing, as phonetic elements and symbols operated across cultures in pre-Columbian Mesoamerica.

Scholars disagree about when the Dresden Codex was made. J. Eric S. Thompson narrows it to 1200 to 1250, while Linton Satterthwaite says no later than 1345. Clive Ruggles suggests it is a copy, originally written between the twelfth and fourteenth centuries.

The Codex Zouche-Nuttall is one of about 16 manuscripts from Mexico that are entirely pre-Columbian in origin. It folds like a screen and is vividly painted on both sides. It is named partly for Zelia Nuttall, who first published it in 1902, and now belongs to the British Museum.

science.text: Obsidian, the volcanic glass used for the blades of the Mesoamerican macuahuitl, can produce an edge sharper than high quality steel razor blades. The macuahuitl was a wooden sword with several obsidian blades embedded in its sides, capable of inflicting serious lacerations, and it was sharp enough to decapitate a man. Its Nahuatl name means "hand-wood".

Maya surgeons did not drill or cut as in central and highland Mexico. They used an abrasive technique that ground away at the back of the skull, thinning the bone and sometimes perforating it. Similar examples are known from Cholula.

Several obsidian mines lay close to the Aztec civilization, both in the Valley of Mexico and in the mountains north of it. Among them were the Sierra de las Navajas, or Razor Mountains, named for their obsidian deposits. The mines supplied the glass for tools and for the macuahuitl, a weapon whose rows of obsidian blades could inflict serious lacerations and was sharp enough to decapitate a man.

Many trepanned skulls from the Maya region date to the Postclassic period, roughly 950 to 1400. They include specimens found at Palenque in Chiapas and others recovered from the Sacred Cenote at Chichen Itza in northern Yucatán. These skulls show the practice was still alive in the medieval Maya world.

Obsidian tools were not only weapons. Obsidian cutting knives, sickles, scrapers, drills, razors and arrow points have all been found in Mesoamerica. Obsidian used in ceramic vessels has also turned up at Aztec sites.

politics.text: The Toltec Empire was a political entity in pre-Hispanic Mexico that gained most of its power in the Postclassic. Its sphere of influence reached as far as the Yucatan Peninsula. Its capital city was Tollan-Xicocotitlan.

The Aztec Empire, also called the Triple Alliance, was an alliance of three Nahua city-states: Mexico-Tenochtitlan, Tetzcoco, and Tlacopan. Together they ruled the area in and around the Valley of Mexico from 1428.

In 1479 the Aztec ruler Axayacatl launched a major invasion of the Purépecha Empire with 32,000 Aztec soldiers. The Purépecha met them just across the border with 50,000 soldiers and scored a resounding victory, killing or capturing over 90% of the Aztec army. Axayacatl himself was wounded in the battle, retreated to Tenochtitlan, and never engaged the Purépecha in battle again.

After the fall of Tollan, many later rulers claimed Toltec lineage to legitimize their power, because Toltec heritage became the standard of the nobility in most of Mesoamerica. Those who did so included the Aztec emperors, the Mixtec kings in Oaxaca, and the K'iche' and Kakchiquel rulers in Guatemala.

The Aztec government had two top figures: the tlatoani, meaning "the one who speaks", handled military affairs, and the cihuacoatl, meaning "woman snake", handled domestic affairs like the food supply and justice. The cihuacoatl was in reality a man, but he wore a woman's dress for ceremonies, sharing his name with a goddess.

The Mexicas founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 as an ally of Azcapotzalco. In 1430 they joined with Texcoco and Tlacopan to wage war against Azcapotzalco and emerged victorious. This gave birth to the Triple Alliance, which replaced the older confederation ruled by the Tecpanecas.

The alliance began as a coalition of three self-governed city-states, but Tenochtitlan became dominant militarily. Over time the lands of the alliance were effectively ruled from Tenochtitlan, while the other partners took subsidiary roles.

After the defeat of the Tepanecs, Itzcoatl and Nezahualcoyotl consolidated power in the Basin of Mexico and began to expand. Their first targets were Coyoacan, Cuauhnahuac and Huaxtepec. These conquests gave the new empire a large influx of tribute, especially agricultural goods.

According to Diego Durán, a second war broke out in Tollan between the followers of Quetzalcoatl and the followers of Tezcatlipoca. It lasted from 1046 to 1110 and ended with the defeat of the followers of Quetzalcoatl. Because of the violence, many supporters of Ce Acatl Topiltzin fled the city, with a sizeable portion of these exiles heading towards the Maya cultural area.

According to Durán, in 1115 tribes from the north (probably Chichimecas, Otomi or Huastecs) attacked the domains of Tollan. In a series of brutal battles at the villages of Nextalpan and Texcalapan, both sides took numerous prisoners and sacrificed them. The Toltecs were defeated in 1116, and Huemac, the priest-king of Tollan, abandoned the city and headed south to Xaltocan, while the majority of the Toltecs split into smaller groups across Mesoamerica. In 1122, shortly after being betrayed by his followers, Huemac hanged himself in Chapultepec.

According to Codex Nuttall, Eight Deer's first military campaign occurred in 1071, when he was eight years old. By 1083 he occupied the throne of Tututepec, near the Pacific coast. Codex Nuttall is the source for these early events of his career.

Moctezuma I died in 1468 and was succeeded by his son Axayacatl. Most of Axayacatl's thirteen-year reign was spent consolidating territory, because Moctezuma and Nezahualcoyotl had expanded so rapidly that many provinces rebelled.

Ethno-religious conflicts between the Nonoalca and the Chichimeca, along with a great famine that struck Tollan from 1070 to 1077, led to migrations from Tollan to other parts of Mesoamerica. One group of Toltec exiles eventually took over the city of Cholula, in present-day Puebla, around 1200. By 1150, Tula was virtually abandoned.

In 1115, tribes from the north attacked the domains of Tollan, and after brutal battles at Nextalpan and Texcalapan, where both sides took and sacrificed numerous prisoners, the Toltecs were defeated in 1116. Huemac, the priest-king of Tollan, abandoned the city and was then deserted by his closest followers, who chose Nauhyotl as their leader. In 1122, shortly after being betrayed by his followers, Huemac hanged himself in Chapultepec. By 1150 Tula was virtually abandoned, and some Toltecs who remained lived under the rule of the nearby city-state of Culhuacán.

In 1455 the Purépecha king Tzitzipandaquare invaded the Toluca Valley, claiming lands previously conquered by Motecuzoma and Itzcoatl. In 1472 Axayacatl re-conquered the region and defended it against Purépecha attempts to take it back.

philosophy.text: The Aztecs called their world Cemanahuac, a name that corresponds to the modern term Mesoamerica. They knew their land was surrounded by the Pacific Ocean, the Gulf of Mexico, and the Caribbean Sea.

The Nahuatl word altepetl, meaning city-state, combines ātl (water) and tepētl (mountain). It rooted the social and political order in the creative powers of a sacred mountain that contained the ancestors, seeds and life-giving forces of the community.

Beyond Eurasia, veneration of the supernatural was used to reinforce power structures, articulate world views and create foundational myths for society. Mesoamerican cosmological narratives are given as an example of this in the post-classical period.

The idea of Cemanahuac is tied to a pyramid-driven philosophy of the Aztecs. Their land sat on top of a natural pyramid, a chain of mountains in central Mexico culminating in Tenochtitlan, just as Aztec leaders sat on top of the Aztec pyramids.

Each altepetl had its own origin story and served as the center of Indigenous identity. Residents named themselves after their altepetl rather than calling themselves Mexicas. The concept is comparable to the Maya cah and the Mixtec ñuu.
A characteristic Nahua mode of thought was to imagine the totality of the people of a region, or even of the world, as a collection of altepetl units. They spoke of other peoples in those terms.

culture.text: The later Aztecs regarded the Toltec as their intellectual and cultural predecessors and described Tula, called Tollan in Nahuatl, as the epitome of civilization. The Nahuatl word Toltekatl came to mean "artisan". The Toltec reached prominence from 950 to 1150 AD.

The Mexica are said to have left Aztlán, though the date is debated, with suggested years of 1064, 1111 and 1168. After much wandering they settled on the Islet of Mexico, under the protection of Tezozómoc, king of the Texpanecas. Tenochtitlan was founded there in 1325.

By the 15th century, a Mayan revival in Yucatan and southern Guatemala and the flourishing of Aztec imperialism enabled a renaissance of fine arts and science. Examples include the Pueblan-Mexica style in pottery, codex illumination and goldwork, and the flourishing of Nahua poetry. The Aztec elite also established botanical institutes.

The later Aztecs considered the Toltec, who reached prominence from 950 to 1150, their intellectual and cultural predecessors. They described Toltec culture, emanating from Tōllān (Tula), as the epitome of civilization.

The Aztec oral and pictographic tradition recorded the history of the Toltec Empire, with lists of rulers and their exploits. Modern scholars disagree over whether these narratives describe real events. All acknowledge a large mythological part, but some think a level of historicity can be salvaged.
Nahuatl, carried by the Toltec and later the Aztec, became a lingua franca throughout Mesoamerica. Even some Mayan states, such as the Kʼicheʼ Kingdom of Qʼumarkaj, adopted it as a prestige language.

Most ethnic groups of central Mexico in the post-classic period shared essential cultural traits of Mesoamerica. These included maize cultivation, a pantheon, a calendric system, and a social division between nobility (pipiltin) and commoners (macehualtin).

In 2007, archaeologists announced they had analyzed the remains of 24 children, aged 5 to 15, found buried together with a figurine of Tlaloc near the ruins of the Toltec capital of Tula. The children had been decapitated, and the remains date to AD 950 to 1150. Archaeologist Luis Gamboa said the only way to explain 24 bodies grouped in one place was to think there was a human sacrifice.

The Purépecha consolidated their state based at Tzintzuntzan and resisted other Mesoamerican states, having little contact with them. Probably because of this isolationist policy, Purépecha is the only Mesoamerican language that shows none of the traits of the Mesoamerican Linguistic Area.
In Nahuatl, the word Tōltēkatl came to mean "artisan". The Aztec name for the Toltecs thus became tied to the idea of skilled craft and refined culture.

Around 1400 CE the Zapotecs of Zaachila moved into the Isthmus of Tehuantepec. They created a wedge of Zapotec-speaking settlements between the Mixe and the Huave, who were pushed into their current territories on the edges of the Isthmus.

Aztec midwives were known as the tlamatlquicitl. They offered medical assistance, analgesics (pain relief medications) and religious rituals during childbirth. Childbirth was a confrontation with the goddess Cihuacoatl: among the Mexica, a woman who died in it was considered temporarily imbued with the power of the goddess. Parts of her body could then be used as a protective amulet or to curse others, so her husband kept vigil by her body for four nights.

According to the historian Enrique Florescano, Mayan sources refer to Chichén Itzá when speaking of the mythical place Zuyua, which is also called Tollan. Several Aztec city-states were likewise called Tollan, "Place of Reeds".
